newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Pension scheme revives spectre of "fund socialism".
newsitem.headline: Pension scheme revives spectre of "fund socialism".

text.p: A Swedish minister's idea for state pension funds to buy more shares, partly to counter growing foreign ownership, has been generally greeted by markets but sent a shiver through company boardrooms.

Finance Minister Erik Asbrink is expected to finalise by next summer his idea to let state pension funds 1-3 invest some of their 550 billion crowns ($83 billion) in Swedish shares, ministry officials told Reuters.
Floating the idea last week, Asbrink said it would help to offset the growing foreign ownership of Swedish shares, now estimated at 30 percent.
"This is sheer hypocrisy," said Lars-Erik Forsgardh, chairman of the Swedish shareholders' association.
"It is a situation (the government) has created itself. If they want to encourage Swedes to buy more shares they should stop discriminating against shareholders through taxation."

Though some analysts said a steady inflow of extra cash would refresh the Stockholm bourse, the Social Democratic minister's words conjured up the ghost of "fund socialism" which once spooked Swedish companies.
Forsgardh recalled that in the late 1970's and early 1980's the Social Democrats created wage-earner funds - now disbanded - from a levy on company profits and allowed them to buy shares.

"We had a very intensive national debate. Companies were afraid that the funds would gradually take over more and more of Swedish industry," Forsgardh said, describing what was dubbed at the time as creeping fund socialism.
At present the 1-3 funds are obliged by law to invest only three percent in property and all the rest in interest-bearing government securities.

Funds number 4 and 5, together holding 55 billion crowns of pensioners' money, already buy shares while fund number six invests in mostly small unlisted companies. Investing in shares traditionally yields higher returns but is riskier.

Asbrink's proposal might be linked with his aim of putting the state budget back in balance by 1997/98, when the government would no longer need the pension funds as ready buyers of short-dated securities.

"Obviously this (proposal) would have a long-term positive effect on the bourse. The inflow of funds would be spread over a long time," brokerage Ohman's head analyst Lars Hoglund said of Asbrink's proposal.
If the 1-3 funds placed 10 percent or 55 billion crowns in shares this would make them one of the biggest institutional investors, Hoglund added.
But few analysts believed that letting funds loose on the share market was the best way to safeguard Swedish corporate ownership and some even questioned whether that was relevant.
They would rather see an easing of the tax burden on individual Swedish share-owners who at present have to pay capital gains tax, dividend tax and even property tax if they have large shareholdings.
"Swedes are taxed at double the rate of other European countries such as Britain, France and Germany," Forsgardh said.
Whatever their investments, the funds will drain steadily from now on because Sweden's ageing population will draw more out in pensions than is paid in by the present workforce.
"If nothing is done, the assets of the pension funds will probably run out around 2010," finance ministry official Stefan Ackerby said.

In the broader context of Asbrink's idea on fund investment, political parties are working on a scheme to replace the funds with a more flexible system in which the individual would have more say in how the assets are managed.
